passage: Jomon, twenty, stood outside the only tailor's shop in Thodupuzha holding two shirt fabrics and his phone. He had already sent photos to four friends. "Hansa, blue or green?" he called to his cousin, who was buying rice across the road. "Blue," she said. A friend texted "green" a minute later, and Jomon's stomach sank. At the co-op bank where he'd just started as a clerk, the manager had called his ledger "a bit untidy", and he had lain awake all night replaying it. Hansa crossed over. "Which one do you like?" Jomon opened his mouth. Nothing came. "I... don't know." "Then stand here till you do," she said, smiling. "No phones." It took four minutes. Green.

qa.q: How many friends had Jomon sent photos to?
qa.a: He had sent photos to four friends.

qa.q: Why did Jomon's stomach sink when a friend texted "green"?
qa.a: The different opinion made him unsure and anxious, because he relies on others' approval to decide.

qa.q: What small step did Hansa suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She asked what he liked and told him to decide without phones, a small chance to trust his own judgement.

qa.q: How might Hansa see Jomon's habit of asking everyone?
qa.a: She seems fond of him but aware he has lost touch with his own preference, so she nudges him kindly.

grounding: A young man in a small town seeks opinions before a simple choice and is crushed by mild criticism, and his cousin nudges him to find his own view.

passage: In a shared flat in Malmö, Tomas, twenty-one, rewrote his university essay introduction for the fifth time. He'd already asked his flatmate Ulla, his mum and two classmates if it was okay. Ulla said it was fine but "a bit long". For the rest of the evening Tomas barely spoke, feeling like a failure. When his mum replied "Brilliant!", he felt great for about ten minutes, then began doubting again. Around midnight Ulla found him still at the kitchen table. "What do you think of it?" she asked. "I don't know. That's the problem." "Try this. Read it out loud and tell me one thing you're proud of in it. Just you." He read. "The last line. I like the last line." "Good. Start there."

qa.q: How many times had Tomas rewritten his introduction?
qa.a: He rewrote his essay introduction for the fifth time.

qa.q: How did Tomas feel after Ulla said the essay was "a bit long"?
qa.a: He felt crushed and like a failure, barely speaking for the rest of the evening.

qa.q: What turning point did Ulla offer, and why is it useful?
qa.a: She asked him to name one thing he was proud of on his own, which starts building his own sense of worth instead of borrowing it.

qa.q: How might Ulla feel seeing her mild comment upset Tomas so much?
qa.a: She may feel surprised and a little guilty, but she stays kind and helps him look inward.

grounding: A student whose mood rises and falls with others' approval begins, with a flatmate's help, to find his own judgement of his work.

passage: At the design agency, Sunaina's intern desk sat next to Karthik's, which was handy, because she asked him about everything. "Is this font okay? Should I say 'Hi' or 'Dear'? Do you think the client will like the blue?" He answered, patiently, eleven times before lunch. At the afternoon review, the creative head said, "The layout's good; the headline's weak." Sunaina nodded, went to the washroom and cried for twenty minutes. The praise had already evaporated; only "weak" remained. Back at her desk she started typing a message to Karthik: "Do you think she hates my work?" Then she stopped, deleted it, and wrote on a sticky note: "What do I think of the headline?"

qa.q: What did the creative head say at the review?
qa.a: "The layout's good; the headline's weak."

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel after the review?
qa.a: She felt crushed and upset, crying for twenty minutes, because the mild criticism outweighed the praise.

qa.q: What small step did Sunaina take towards an inner sense of worth?
qa.a: She deleted the message asking Karthik and wrote a note asking what she herself thought of the headline.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel after answering eleven questions before lunch?
qa.a: Karthik is patient but may feel a bit tired, and might worry that Sunaina doubts her own judgement.

grounding: Shows a young adult who asks for approval before every choice and is crushed by mild criticism, starting to build inner worth.

passage:
Dear Joseph-sir,
You once told our Class 12 that I'd go far because I "always ask good questions". I've been thinking about that. In college I ask questions about everything, but mostly one: "Is this okay?" I send my roommate my assignments before I submit. I ask three friends which shirt to wear to a seminar. Last week a professor wrote "argument unclear" next to one paragraph, and I didn't sleep. The good comments above it didn't count at all. It's like praise wears off in an hour and I need more. So I've started a small experiment: one decision a day with no asking. Today it was the shirt. It was fine. I thought you'd like to know.
Kishore

qa.q: What did the professor write next to one paragraph?
qa.a: "argument unclear"

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after the professor's comment?
qa.a: Kishore felt so upset and anxious that sleep wouldn't come, while the good comments seemed to count for nothing.

qa.q: Why is Kishore's small experiment a good step?
qa.a: Making one decision a day without asking slowly builds trust in Kishore's own judgement.

qa.q: How might Joseph-sir feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Joseph-sir would likely feel touched to be trusted and glad Kishore is working on it.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who needs approval for every decision and is crushed by mild criticism, beginning to build inner worth.

passage: You'll laugh, but I asked six people whether I should cut my hair. Six. That's how all of first year went for me. I'm Manoj, by the way, twenty, and I couldn't choose a lunch order without checking what my friend Avni was getting. When she said, gently, that my presentation was "a bit long", I went home feeling like the floor had dropped away. Three hours of replaying it. A compliment from her lasted, what, a morning? Then I needed another. The college counsellor said something I keep thinking about: "Approval from outside is like sugar. Sweet, and then it's gone." So now I practise. Small things. I chose this shirt myself. I actually like it.

qa.q: How many people did Manoj ask about the haircut?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel after Avni called the presentation a bit long?
qa.a: Manoj felt crushed, as if the floor had dropped away, replaying it for three hours.

qa.q: What is Manoj doing to build an inner sense of worth?
qa.a: Practising small choices alone, like picking a shirt, after the counsellor's advice about outside approval.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt if she knew her gentle comment caused three hours of replaying?
qa.a: Avni might feel surprised and sorry, since she meant it kindly.

grounding: Shows a young adult for whom approval fades quickly and mild criticism crushes, practising small independent choices.

passage:
Monday: Before her internship interview, Devika sent photos of three kurtas to six friends. When Anand replied, "The blue is a bit dull," her stomach dropped. She changed twice and nearly cried.
Thursday: Choosing her final-year project topic, she reached for her phone to ask the group. She stopped and put it face down. Instead she wrote three reasons she liked the topic on urban gardens, in her own words, and chose it.
Two weeks later: Her professor said, "Your introduction is weak." The old sting came back, hot and fast. She wanted to message five people for comfort. She opened her notebook to the three reasons instead, read them twice, and started rewriting the introduction. By evening she felt steadier, even a little proud.

qa.q: How many friends did Devika send kurta photos to?
qa.a: Six friends.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when Anand said the blue was a bit dull?
qa.a: She felt crushed and anxious; her stomach dropped, she changed twice and nearly cried.

qa.q: What did Devika do on Thursday that started building her own sense of worth?
qa.a: She put the phone face down and wrote her own three reasons for the topic, choosing it without asking the group.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had messaged five people after the professor's comment?
qa.a: She might have felt better briefly, but the comfort would fade, and she would miss the chance to steady herself with her own reasons.

grounding: Shows a young adult who seeks opinions before every choice and is crushed by mild criticism, slowly building an inner sense of worth.
